label: Main Thm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Main Thm}
    Let $M(x,y) = m(d(x,y))$ be a radial symbol on a tree and $T_m$ the corresponding even Fourier multiplier on the torus $\mathbf{T}$. Then, for every $1 < p < \infty$ we have 
    \[
        \big\| S_M \colon S_p(X) \to S_p(X) \big\|_\mathrm{cb} \, \lesssim \, p_\ast^2 \, \big\| T_m \colon L_p(\mathbf{T}) \to L_p(\mathbf{T}) \big\|_\mathrm{cb},
    \]
    where $p_\ast := \max\{p,\tfrac{p}{p-1}\}$. If $X$ has infinite diameter, the reciprocal inequality also holds 
    \[
        \big\| S_M \colon S_p(X) \to S_p(X) \big\|_\mathrm{cb} \ge \big\| T_m \colon L_p(\mathbf{T}) \to L_p(\mathbf{T}) \big\|_\mathrm{cb}.
    \]

label: Martingale transform
title: Proof
body_md:
Given $k\geq 0$, consider the equivalence relation
\[
x\sim_k y \ \Leftrightarrow \ x=y \ \text{or } |x\wedge y| \geq k.
\]
Let $\mathcal{P}_k$ be the partition of $X$ induced by $\sim_k$ and define the map
\[
\mathbf{E}_k(A) = \sum_{\Sigma \in \mathcal{P}_k} P_\Sigma A P_\Sigma = \Big[ \mathbf{1}_{x\sim_k y}\,A_{x,y} \Big]_{x,y},
\]
where $P_\Sigma$ is the orthogonal projection from $\ell_2(X)$ onto $\ell_2(\Sigma)$. The map $\mathbf{E}_0$ is just the identity and each $\mathbf{E}_k$ defines a conditional expectation onto decreasing matrix subalgebras of $\mathcal{B}(\ell_2(X))$. It is therefore clear that $(\mathbf{E}_k(A))_{k \ge 0}$ defines a decreasing noncommutative martingale. Note as well that these conditional expectations approximate the diagonal restriction $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{diag}$---the only trace preserving conditional expectation onto the subalgebra of diagonal matrices---since the intersection of all  partitions $\mathcal{P}_k$ is the partition into singletons. If $\mathbf{d}_{k} = \mathbf{E}_k - \mathbf{E}_{k+1}$ for $k\geq 0$, then it is clear that we may write
\[
    A = \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{diag}}(A) + \sum_{k\geq 0} \mathbf{d}_{k} (A).
\]
Next, if we set $\mathcal{D}_z = \mathrm{diag}(z^{|\cdot|})$ we claim that
\begin{equation} \label{Martingale transform}
   \mathcal{C}_z(A)= \mathcal{D}_z \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{diag}}(A) + \sum_{k\geq 0} z^{k} \mathbf{d}_{k} (A).
\end{equation}   
Indeed, $\mathcal{C}_z$ acts by pointwise multiplication with $z^{|\cdot|}$ on the diagonal, whereas for $x\neq y$, we have $x\sim_k y \ \text{and } x\not\sim_{k+1} y \ \Leftrightarrow \ |x\wedge y| = k$. Thus, the off-diagonal entries of $\mathbf{d}_{k} (A)$ are exactly $\mathbf{1}_{|x\wedge y|=k}A_{x,y}$ while the diagonal ones vanish. Finally, the statement follows from the martingale transform inequality \eqref{MartTransforms} and the identity \eqref{Martingale transform}  
\[
    \| \mathcal{C}_z(A) \|_p 
    \leq \| A \|_p + \Big\| \sum_{k \geq 0} z^k \mathbf{d}_{k} (A) \Big\|_p 
    \lesssim \, \max\{ p, p' \} \, \Big( \sup_{k \geq 0} |z^k| \Big) \, \| A \|_p =  \, p_\ast \, \| A \|_p. 
\]
The same argument gives cb-bounds. This follows from the fact that martingale transforms are completely bounded, which follows automatically by taking the expectations $\mathbf{E}_k \otimes \mathrm{id}_{M_m}$ instead.

label: eq:Intertwining
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Delta \colon S_p(X) \to L_p(\mathbf{T};S_p(X))$ be the map sending $A$ to the function $z \mapsto \Delta_z(A)$. Then, we will see that
    \[
        \frac1{c(p)} \, \| A \|_p \lesssim \| \Delta(A) \|_{L_p(\mathbf{T}; S_p)} \lesssim c(p) \, \| A \|_p,
    \]
    with $c(p) = p_\ast$. Indeed, the fact that $\Delta$ is bounded follows from Lemma \ref{KeyLemma} and the identity $\Delta_z = \mathcal{U}_z \circ \mathcal{C}_{z^{-2}}$. Integrating on $z$ yields
    \[
        \| \Delta(A) \|_{L_p(\mathbf{T};S_p)} = \Big( \int_\mathbf{T} \| \Delta_z(A) \|_{S_p}^p \, dz \Big)^{\frac1p} \lesssim c(p) \Big( \int_\mathbf{T} \| A \|_{S_p}^p \, dz \Big)^{\frac1p} = c(p) \, \| A \|_{S_p}.
    \]
    To see the lower bound, just notice that $A = \Delta_{\bar z} \Delta_z(A)$ and integrate on the torus $\mathbf{T}$. Now, given an even function $m: \mathbf{Z} \to \mathbf{C}$ satisfying $M(x,y) = m(d(x,y))$ as in the statement, we have that the following diagram commutes
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:Intertwining}
        \begin{tikzcd}
            S_p(X) \arrow[r, "\Delta"] \arrow[d, "S_M"] & L_p(\mathbf{T};S_p(X)) \arrow[d, "T_m \otimes \mathrm{id}"]\\
            S_p(X) \arrow[r, "\Delta"] & L_p(\mathbf{T};S_p(X))
        \end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}  
In other words, we have $\Delta \circ S_M = (T_m \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta$. Since $\Delta$ is a quasi-isometry, the boundedness of $T_m \otimes \mathrm{id}$ implies the boundedness of $S_M$ with constant $c(p)^2$. The complete bound for $S_M$ follows from the fact that $\Delta$ and its inverse are completely bounded. To see the second assertion, let us first assume that $X$ contains an infinite ray starting at $o \in X$. Let us denote by $\rho = (\rho_n)_{n \geq 0}$ the sequence of nodes of this ray. The restriction of $M(x,y)$ to $\rho$ is just
    \[
        M(\rho_n, \rho_\ell) = m(d(\rho_n, \rho_\ell)) = m(|n-\ell|).
    \]
Restriction of Schur multipliers preserves the norm on Schatten $p$-classes \cite[Section 1]{LaffSall2011}. It turns out moreover that the restriction to $\rho \times \rho$ gives a Herz-Schur multiplier over $S_p(\mathbf{Z})$. Thus, by Fourier-Schur transference \cite{NeuRic2011} over $\mathbf{Z}$ we obtain that: 
\[
    \big\| S_M \colon S_p(X) \to S_p(X) \big\| \geq \big\| S_{M_{\mid_{\rho \times \rho}}} \! \colon S_p(\mathbf{N}_0) \to S_p(\mathbf{N}_0) \big\| \geq \big\| T_m \colon L_p(\mathbf{T}) \to L_p(\mathbf{T}) \big\|,
\]
where we have used that, for even symbols $m$, the Herz-Schur multiplier norm is detected by just the positive entries on $S_p(\mathbf{N}_0)$. This allows us to conclude. Observe as well that the inequalities above work similarly well for completely bounded norms. Now, if $X$ doesn't contain an infinite ray, because the diameter is infinite, it has to contain arbitrarily long geodesic segments starting at $o \in X$. By restricting to those segments and using that the $L_p$-norm of $T_m$ can be approximated when restricting the multiplier to $[0,N]$ as $N \to \infty$ we can conclude.

title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont
The lower estimate holds as well in the category of Banach spaces---replacing cb by ordinary norms---whereas our argument for the upper bound uses critically the cb-boundedness of the Fourier multiplier $T_m \colon L_p(\mathbf{T}) \to L_p(\mathbf{T})$. If the upper estimate also held for Banach space norms, $S_p$-bounded radial Schur multipliers on unbounded trees would coincide with the class of $L_p$-bounded Fourier multipliers on $\mathbf{T}$. As pointed by Patrick Poissel, according to the existence from \cite[Chapter 8]{Pi1998} of Fourier $L_p$-multipliers on $\mathbf{T}$ which fail complete boundedness, this would imply the existence of Schur $S_p$-multipliers which fail to be completely $S_p$-bounded, solving an open problem posed by Pisier in 1998. We refer to \cite{HuangSukochevTomskova2026Schur} for recent progress on the problem.

label: rmk:Optimalcp
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:Optimalcp} \normalfont
    While the constant in \eqref{SphericalInequality} can easily be seen to be optimal, at present, wo do not know whether the $p$-dependent constant in Theorem \ref{Main Thm} can be improved. The fact that Theorem \ref{Main Thm} fails for $p=\infty$ implies that the constant must diverge when $p\to 1^+$ or $p \to \infty$. It is also evidently self-dual. Thus, it would be natural to conjecture that it can be lowered from $O(p_\ast^2)$ to $O(p_\ast)$, but we have only partial results in that direction. A naïve approach would consist on noticing that, if $\mathrm{ev}_0: C(\mathbf{T}) \to \mathbf{C}$ is the state given by evaluation at $0 \in \mathbf{T}$, then formally it is satisfied that 
    \[
        (\mathrm{ev}_0 \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (T_m \otimes \mathrm{id}) \Delta = S_M, \, 
        \text{ where } M(x,y) = m(d(x,y)).
    \]
    However, $\mathrm{ev}_0$ is unbounded on $L_p(\mathbf{T})$. Similarly, one can show that, for every $A \in S_p(X)$, $z \mapsto \Delta_z(A)$ is norm continuous in $S_p(X)$. This follows from a careful application of Burkholder's inequality for martingale transforms \eqref{MartTransforms}. But, while this gives that $\Delta \colon S_p(X) \to C(\mathbf{T}; S_p(X))$ is a bounded map, in order to apply the intertwining identity we will need for $T_m$ to be completely bounded on $C(\mathbf{T})$, leaving only non-singular multipliers obtained when $\widehat{m}$ is a finite signed measure in $M(\mathbf{T})$. A more sophisticated approach will be considered in a follow-up paper.

label: lem:Derivatives
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Derivatives}
    Given a tree $X$, the multiplier $\Delta_z \colon S_p(X) \to S_p(X)$, given by $\Delta_z(A)_{x, y} = z^{d(x,y)}$ for $|z| \leq 1$ is bounded for every $p \in (1,\infty)$ with the same bound as in \eqref{SphericalInequality}. Furthermore, the map $z \mapsto \Delta_z$ is holomorphic over the open disk and, given any $0 \leq r_0 < 1$, we have that
    \[
        \sup_{|z| \leq r_0} \Big\| \frac{\partial}{ \partial \, z} \Delta_z \colon S_p(X) \to S_p(X) \Big\|_\mathrm{cb} 
        \, \lesssim_{(r_0)} \, 
        \max \{ p, p'\} \quad \text{for every} \quad 1< p < \infty. 
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is immediate. First, notice that if $|z| \leq 1$, then $z = \rho \, u$ with $|u|=1$. If $|\rho|=1$ there is nothing to prove. Meanwhile, if $\rho < 1$ we have that $\Delta_z$ is the composition of $\Delta_u$ and the radial Schur multiplier $\rho^{d(x,y)}$, which is positive definite and thus completely bounded for every $p \in [1,\infty]$.
    The second inequality follows from the fact that the symbol $z \mapsto z^{d(x,y)}$ is bounded and holomorphic when $z$ in the unit disk and that the derivative of an holomorphic map is also holomorphic. Observe as well that this is equivalent to the $S_p$-boundedness of the radial Schur symbols $d(x,y) \, z^{d(x,y)}$ for $|z| \leq r_0 < 1$.

label: eq:Annulus
title: Proof
body_md:
We divide the proof into two steps. First, we will show that $z \in \mathbf{D}_q$ implies that both roots satisfy $|\alpha_\pm| \leq 1$ and then, we will see that \eqref{eq:ClosedFormulaSph} implies $S_p$-boundedness when $|\alpha_\pm|\leq 1$. For the first claim, notice that $\alpha_+ \alpha_- = \tfrac1{q}$. Thus, if one of the roots satisfies $|\alpha_+| \leq 1$ then the other satisfies $|\alpha_-|\geq \frac1{q}$, thus
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:Annulus}
        \Big\{ z : |\alpha_+| \leq 1 \text{ and } |\alpha_-| \leq 1 \Big\}
        \; = \; \Big\{ z : \tfrac1{q} \leq |\alpha_+| \leq 1 \Big\} =: \mathbf{A}_q.
    \end{equation}
    The formulas for $\alpha_\pm$ in terms of $z$ are obtained after solving $\alpha$ in terms of $z$ the characteristic equation. If we instead express $z$ in terms of $\alpha$, we obtain the so-called Joukowski map
    \[
        J_q(\alpha) = \frac1{q+1} \Big( q \alpha + \frac1{\alpha}\Big)
    \]
   of which $z \mapsto \alpha_\pm(z)$ are the two branches of its inverse. Thus, we can characterize the set in \eqref{eq:Annulus} as the image under $J_q$ the the annulus $\mathbf{A}_q$. Now, elementary computations show that $J_q$ maps $\mathbf{A}_q$ into $\overline{\mathbf{D}}_q$. In fact every concentric circle is mapped into an ellipse up to the circle $\{|z|= \tfrac1{q}\}$, which is mapped to the interval $[-c_q, +c_q] \subseteq \mathbf{D}_q$.
    
    Now, we just need to show that the formula \eqref{eq:ClosedFormulaSph} induces uniformly bounded $S_p$ multipliers when $|\alpha_\pm| \leq 1$. Let us first deal with the case of two different roots. Regrouping terms gives
    \[
        \mathring{\varphi}_z(n)
        =
        \frac12 (\alpha_+^n+\alpha_-^n)
        +b_z \, \frac{\alpha_+^n-\alpha_-^n}{\alpha_+-\alpha_-}
        \quad \text{where} \quad b_z=\frac{q-1}{2q}z.
    \]
    The first summand induces the radial Schur multiplier $\Delta_{\alpha_+} + \Delta_{\alpha_-}$, which is uniformly bounded on the disk by Lemma \ref{lem:Derivatives}. For the second term, first notice that the coefficient $b_z$ is bounded on $\overline{\mathbf{D}}_q$ and thus irrelevant. Next, fix $\delta > 0$ to be determined later. We separate the cases $|\alpha_+ - \alpha_-| \geq \delta$ and $|\alpha_+ - \alpha_-| <\delta$. In the first case, we have that
    \[
        \Big\| \frac{\Delta_{\alpha_+}-\Delta_{\alpha_-}}{\alpha_+-\alpha_-} \Big\|_{\mathcal{C B}(S_p)} \leq \frac{2}{\delta} \sup_{z \in \overline{\mathbf{D}}_q} \| \Delta_z \|_{\mathcal{C B}(S_p)}.
    \]
    For the second case, using that $\alpha_+ \, \alpha_- = \tfrac1{q}$, we get that if $\alpha_+$, $\alpha_-$ are close enough, then their modulus should be of the order of $\tfrac1{\sqrt{q}} < 1$ and thus, they can be taken to lay in a closed disk $|z|\leq r_\delta < 1$. By the mean value theorem we get
    \[
        \frac{\Delta_{\alpha_+}-\Delta_{\alpha_-}}{\alpha_+-\alpha_-} = \int_0^1 \frac{\partial \Delta_z}{ \partial \, z} \big( \alpha_- + t (\alpha_+ - \alpha_-) \big)\, dt.
    \]
    Taking operator norms and applying Lemma \ref{lem:Derivatives} we can conclude.
    For the double multiplicity case, it is enough to consider the radial multiplier of symbol
    \[
        M(x,y) = \Big(1+\frac{q-1}{q+1}\,d(x,y)\Big) \, q^{-\frac{d(x,y)}{2}}.
    \]
    Its $S_p$-boundedness follows from that of $d(x,y)\rho^{-d(x,y)}$, which is obtained from Lemma \ref{lem:Derivatives}.

The implication \ref{itm:HoroballvsBall.2} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{itm:HoroballvsBall.1} has been already justified. For the converse, consider a branch $\rho = (\rho_n)_{n \ge 1} \in \partial \mathbf{F}_r$ and let $x_n$ be the last letter of $\rho_n$. Fix a positive integer $R$ and take the partition $\mathbf{F}_r = \mathrm{A}_R \cup \mathrm{B}_R \cup \{e\}$ with $\mathrm{A}_R$ the words starting with $x_{R+1}$ or $x_R^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{B}_R$ the complementary set in $\mathbf{F}_r \setminus \{e\}$. Let $x_\perp$ be a generator or an inverse of a generator not belonging to $\{ x_R, x_{R+1}^{-1}, x_{R+2} \}$. Then 
\[
    T_{\1_{B_R}} \Big( \sum_{w \in \mathbf{F}_2} a_w \lambda_w \Big) = a_e \lambda_e  + \lambda_{\rho_{R+1} x_\perp}^* T_{m_\rho} \Big( \sum_{w \in \mathrm{A}_R} a_w \lambda_{\rho_{R+1} x_{\perp} w} \Big) + \lambda_{\rho_R}^* T_{m_\rho} \Big( \sum_{w \in \mathrm{B}_R} a_w \lambda_{\rho_R w} \Big).
\]
Since $\mathrm{A}_R$ and $\mathrm{B}_R$ define free Hilbert transforms  \cite{MeiRicard2017FreeHilb}, we get

\]

label: Rem-Curvature
title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont \label{Rem-Curvature} 
Let us fix a parameter $q>1$ and set $|w|_q$ to be the $q$-th analog of the word length. Namely, if $w = g_{j_1}^{k_1} g_{j_2}^{k_2} \cdots g_{j_n}^{k_n}$ is any word written in terms of the generators $g_1, g_2, \ldots$ with $j_1 \neq j_2 \neq \ldots \neq j_n$ and integer exponents, we define 
\[
    |w|_q = \Big( \sum_{\ell=1}^n |k_\ell|^q \Big)^\frac1{q}
\]
so that $|\cdot|_1$ recovers the word length. In \cite{MixedNorm2026} we use a rescaling argument to disprove the uniform $S_p$-boundedness of free $q$-balls for every $p \neq 2$ and $q>1$. It essentially shows that rescaled large free $q$-balls approximate sets admitting 2-dimensional sections which fail the zero-curvature condition in \cite{Parcet2024Idempotentschur} characterizing Schur idempotents. By the easy direction in Fourier-Schur transference---valid for nonamenable groups---free $q$-balls also fail uniform $L_p$-boundedness in the Fourier setting for $p \neq 2$. 
Before becoming aware of Theorem \ref{CorFree}\ref{itm:CorFree1}, one might have been tempted to treat the case \(q=1\) by adapting the preceding argument. Again by Fourier-Schur transference, this would imply the solution to the free ball multiplier problem left open in \cite{Kuhn1984Convergence, BoFen2006}. To our surprise, Theorem \ref{Main Thm} shows a drastic change of regime at the endpoint $q=1$ and free balls turn out to be curved in the Fourier setting---at least for $|\frac12 - \frac1p| > \frac16$--- but flat in the Schur sense of \cite{Parcet2024Idempotentschur}. It is a major challenge to find sufficient evidence of curvature---in the sense of  \cite{Fef1971}---to disprove the uniform \(L_p\)-boundedness of Fourier projections onto free balls for \(p\) close to \(2\).

label: eq:theta-measure
title: Proof
body_md:
Define $\widetilde{Q}_0 := \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}}$ and $\widetilde{Q}_n := Q_n$ for $n \geq 1$. This gives 
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_u(s) \; := \; \sum_{n = 0}^\infty u^n \widetilde{Q}_n(s)
        & = & \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}} + 2 \sqrt{\tau} s u + \sum_{n = 2}^\infty \widetilde{Q}_n(s) u^n\\
        & = & \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}} + 2 \sqrt{\tau} s u + \sum_{n = 2}^\infty u^n \big[ 2 s \, \widetilde{Q}_{n-1}  (s)- \widetilde{Q}_{n-2}(s) \big] \\
        & = & \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}} + 2 \sqrt{\tau} s u + 2 s u \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \widetilde{Q}_{n} (s) u^n - u^2 \sum_{n=0}^\infty \widetilde{Q}_{n}(s) u^n\\
         & = & \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}} + 2 \sqrt{\tau} s u + 2 s u \, \Big[ \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_u(s) - \frac1{\sqrt{\tau}} \Big] - u^2 \, \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_u(s).
    \end{eqnarray*}
Identity \eqref{eq:Gformula} follows rearranging and using $$\mathcal{G}_u(s) = \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_u(s) + \Big( 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}} \Big).$$
Next, we do the change of variable $s = \cos \theta$ to obtain 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:theta-measure}
        d\nu_\tau(\cos\theta)
        =\frac{2\tau}{\pi}\,
        \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{1-4\tau(1-\tau)\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta.
    \end{equation}
    Since $\tau >\tfrac12$, we easily get $d\nu_\tau(\cos\theta) \simeq_{(r)} \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta$ since $4\tau(1-\tau) < 1$ and the denominator in \eqref{eq:theta-measure}  
is bounded below by a nonzero constant. Similarly, the numerator in \eqref{eq:Gformula} is comparable to a constant depending on $\tau$. Indeed, the function $F_{\tau}(s,u) = 1+2(\sqrt{\tau}-1)su+(1-\frac1{\sqrt{\tau}})u^2$ is clearly bounded above by 4 and observe that $$|F_\tau(s,u)-1| = \Big| (\sqrt{\tau}-1) u (2s+\frac{u}{\sqrt{\tau}}) \Big| \le (1-\sqrt{\tau}) \Big( 2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}} \Big).$$ This implies $|F_\tau(s,u)| \ge 1-(1-\sqrt{\tau})(2+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}}) = 2 \sqrt{\tau} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}} = C_\tau > 0$ and we get for $1\leq p<\infty$
$$\|\mathcal{G}_u \|_{p}^p \, \simeq_{(r,p)} \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin^2 \theta \, d\theta}{|1-ue^{i\theta}|^p|1-ue^{-i\theta}|^p} \qquad \mbox{for any} \qquad |u|\leq1.$$
Now we can prove the two final statements: 
    
    To prove {\ref{itm:pNorm1}}, fix $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$ and take $u=\beta e^{i\alpha}$.  Near $\theta=\alpha$
    \[
        \big| 1-\beta e^{i(\alpha-\theta)} \big|^2 \simeq (1-\beta)^2+(\theta-\alpha)^2,
    \]
    while the other factor in the denominator and $\sin\theta$ remain bounded above and below up to some constants depending on $\alpha$.  Therefore, since the integral above is smaller when $|\alpha - \theta|$ is large, we get the norm equivalence
    \[
        \|\mathcal{G}_{\beta e^{i\alpha}}\|_p^p
        \simeq_{(r,p,\alpha)}
        \int_{-1}^{1}\frac{d v}{((1-\beta)^2+v^2)^{p/2}}
    \]
    and we obtain the norm equivalence \eqref{eq:interior-asymptotics} by integrating the right hand side.

    For {\ref{itm:pNorm2}}, take $u=\beta \in(0,1)$.  Near $\theta=0$
    \[
        \big| 1-2\beta\cos\theta+\beta^2 \big|
        = \big| 1-\beta e^{i\theta} \big|^2
         \simeq (1-\beta)^2+\theta^2.
    \]
    Using the quadratic vanishing of $\sin^2 \theta$ near $\theta = 0$, one obtains
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-integral}
        \|\mathcal G_{\beta} \|_p^p
         \simeq_{(r,p)}
        1+\int_0^1\frac{\theta^2}{((1-\beta)^2+\theta^2)^p}\,d\theta.
    \end{equation}
    Again, we obtain the norm equivalence \eqref{eq:endpoint-asymptotics} by integrating the right hand side.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have 
\[
  L_2(\mathrm{G})\simeq \ell_2(\mathrm{G}/\mathrm{K}) \otimes_2 L_2(\mathrm{K}) = \ell_2(X_q) \otimes_2 L_2(\mathrm{K}),
\]
so that $S_p(\mathrm{G}) \simeq S_p(X_q) \otimes_p S_p(\mathrm{K})$. Since $\ell_\mathrm{Car}(g^{-1}h) = d(g^{-1}h\mathrm{K}, \mathrm{K}) = d(h\mathrm{K}, g\mathrm{K})$, the complete boundedness of $S_{M_z}$ reduces to that of the Schur multiplier $\Delta_z$ with symbol $z^{d(x,y)}$, considered in Section \ref{Sect1}. For the unboundedness of the Fourier multipliers $T_{m_z}$, we follow the strategy in Subsection \ref{SphericalSect} using that the convolution algebra of $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant functions is Abelian. When taking weak-$\ast$ closures, this $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant algebra can be identified with the finite corner
\[
    \mathcal{L}(\mathrm{K} \backslash \mathrm{G}/\mathrm{K}) \simeq p_\mathrm{K} \, \mathcal{L} \mathrm{G} \, p_\mathrm{K} \qquad \mbox{ where } \qquad p_\mathrm{K} = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \lambda_k \, d \mu_\mathrm{K}(k),
\]
and $\mu_\mathrm{K}$ is the normalized Haar measure on $\mathrm{K}$. The trace of $p_\mathrm{K}$ is finite and thus we can identify such corner with its Gelfand spectrum and $\tau$ restricted to the $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant part with a finite measure
\begin{equation}
     \big( p_\mathrm{K} \, \mathcal{L} \mathrm{G} \, p_\mathrm{K}, \tau \big) \longrightarrow L_\infty\big( [-2,2]; \mu_q\big),
\end{equation}
where 
\[
d\mu_q(x)=
 \frac{q+1}{(q^{1/2}+q^{-1/2})^2-x^2}
 \frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2\pi}\,
\,dx \qquad \mbox{with} \quad -2 \le x \le 2.
\]
The explicit form of this isomorphism can be given by the spherical transform, which sends a suitable normalization of the characteristic functions of the spheres to the corresponding family of orthogonal polynomials. Namely, the $n$-th sphere
\[
    \mathrm{K} \, \begin{bmatrix} q^n&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} \, \mathrm{K}
\]
is sent to $P_n(s)$, where we set 
\[
    P_0(s)=1,\qquad P_1(s)=s, \qquad P_n(s)=U_n(s/2)-q^{-1}U_{n-2}(s/2),
\]
where $U_n$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind and $n\ge2$, we refer to \cite{HasegawaSaigoSaitoSugiyama2018} and references therein for further details. Now, explicit computing of the generating function for $(P_n(s))_{n \geq 0}$ and its $L_p(\mu_q)$-norms for $\beta$ and $\beta e^{i \alpha}$ gives the result as in Lemma \ref{prop:generating}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us denote $\mathrm{G} = \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{R})$ and $\mathrm{K} = \mathrm{PSO}(2)$. Since $m_s\colon \mathrm{G} \to \mathbf{C}$ is $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant, $M_s(g,h) = m_s(g^{-1}h)$ naturally lifts to the homogeneous space $\mathrm{G}/\mathrm{K}$ as $\widetilde{M}_s$. Identifying $\mathrm{K} \backslash \mathrm{G}$ with the hyperbolic upper half space $\mathbf{H}^2$, and using that $\mathrm{K} \curvearrowright \mathrm{G}/\mathrm{K}$ acts by hyperbolic rotations around $i \in \mathbf{H}^2$, we obtain that $\widetilde{M}_s$ is a radial multiplier on the Riemannian distance below
    \[
        \widetilde{M}_s(x,y) = e^{ 2 \pi i \, s \, d_{\mathbf{H}^2}(x,y)}.
    \]
    We have the following limit, which holds uniformly over compact subsets of $\mathbf{H}^2 \times \mathbf{H}^2$:
    \[
        \lim_{\delta \to 0^+} \frac{d_{\mathbf{H}^2}\big( \exp_i(\delta v), \, \exp_i(\delta w) \big)}{\delta} = |w - v|,
    \]
    where $v,w$ are tangent vectors at $i \in \mathbf{H}^2$ and $\exp_i$ is the geodesic flow starting at $i$. Given $x \in \mathbf{H}^2$ there is a unique geodesic connecting it with $i$. Let us denote by $\phi_\delta(x)$ the change of variable given by sending $x$ to the point $\phi_\delta(x)$ along the geodesic connecting $i$ and $x$ whose distance from $i$ is a fraction $\delta$ of $d_{\mathbf{H}^2}(x,i)$. That is
    \[
        \phi_\delta(\exp_i(v)) := \exp_i(\delta v).
    \]
    The map $\phi_t$ is a smooth diffeomorphism and, in particular, it preserves the measure class. By \cite[Lemma 2.1.]{Parcet2024Idempotentschur} the operator $S_p$ norms of $\widetilde{M}_s(x,y)$ and $\widetilde{M}_s(\phi_t(x),\phi_t(y))$ coincide. Assuming by contradiction that the supremum on \eqref{eq:NonUniformSL2} is bounded, we can take $s = \tfrac{1}{\delta}$, so that
    \[
        \lim_{\delta \to 0^+} e^{ 2 \pi i \, \tfrac{1}{\delta} \, d_{\mathbf{H}^2}(\phi_\delta(x),\phi_\delta(y))} 
        = e^{ 2 \pi i |v_x - v_y|},
    \]
    where $v_x$ represents the tangent vector of the unique geodesic from $i$ to $x$. By assumption, the $\delta$-dependent family of Schur multipliers above is uniformly bounded. The limit converges uniformly over compact sets. Thus, the limit is also an $S_p$-bounded Schur multiplier by  \cite[Theorem 1.19]{LaffSall2011}. But, since $\mathbf{R}^2$ is an amenable group, by \cite{CasSall2015}, that would imply the boundedness of the half-wave propagator $e^{2 \pi i \, |\xi|}$, which is known to be unbounded as a Fourier multiplier on $L_p(\mathbf{R}^2)$. We refer to \cite{Miyachi1980,Peral1980} or to \cite{BeltranRoosRutarSeeger2025} for a more modern treatment.

label: rmk:IntertwiningSp
title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont
    \label{rmk:IntertwiningSp}
    There is an alternative proof of Theorem \ref{ThmBallsSL2}. Indeed, assume by contradiction that the family $\{H_{m_s}: s \in \mathbf{R} \}$ is indeed uniformly bounded in $S_p(\mathrm{G})$. Then, it induces a bounded map $\Lambda \colon S_p(\mathrm{G}) \to L_\infty(\mathbf{R}; S_p(\mathrm{G}))$ given by sending $A \in S_p(\mathrm{G})$ to the function $s \mapsto H_{m_s}(A)$. This map doesn't preserve the Lebesgue measure in $\mathbf{R}$, since it is not a probability measure. Therefore it does not immediately extend to $L_p(\mathbf{R}; S_p)$. However this can be fixed by choosing Gaussian probability measures $d \mu_\delta(x) = \gamma_\delta(x) dx$ of variance $\frac1{\delta}$. Then, by the finiteness of $\mu_\delta$, we have that $\Lambda_\delta: S_p(\mathrm{G}) \to L_\infty(\mathbf{R}, d\mu_\delta; S_p(\mathrm{G}))$ are quasi-isometries. Now, we can use that multiplication by a Gaussian intertwines in $L_p$-sense with the action of the Fourier multiplier in the limit as $\delta \to 0$, ie:
    \[
        {\delta^{-\frac1{2p}}} \, \big\| \gamma_\delta^{\frac1{p}} (T_\varphi \otimes \mathrm{id})[F] -  (T_\varphi \otimes \mathrm{id})[\gamma_\delta^{\frac1{p}} F] \big\|_{L_p(\mathbf{R};S_p)} \to 0,
        \; \text{ as } \, \delta \to 0^+.
    \]
    This property goes back to de Leeuw's celebrated paper \cite{Lee1965}, but the exact same argument needed here can be found in \cite[Proposition 1.7]{ParcetSLn2018} or \cite[Section 2.5]{ParRog2016Hilbert}. Thus, in the limit $\delta \to 0$,  $\Lambda_\delta$ intertwines $H_{\varphi \circ L}$ with $T_{\varphi} \otimes \mathrm{id}_{S_p}$ and thus
    \[
        \big\| H_{\varphi \circ L}\colon S_p(\mathrm{G}) \to S_p(\mathrm{G}) \big\|  \; \lesssim \; \big\| T_\varphi: L_p(\mathbf{R}) \to L_p(\mathbf{R})\big \|_{\mathrm{cb}}.
    \]
    Taking $\varphi = \1_{[-R,R]}$, we would get the $L_p$-boundedness of the multiplier induced by geodesic balls on $\mathbf{H}^2$, which contradicts the characterization of Schur idempotents with a smooth boundary in \cite{Parcet2024Idempotentschur}.

label: lem:KbiinInduced
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:KbiinInduced}
    Given $m \in \ell_\infty(\Gamma)$, its amplification $\widehat{m}$ is continuous, bounded and $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Omega$ be the range of the section modulo null sets and take $d=\mu(\Omega)$. Define the bounded measurable function $F_m(\gamma \omega)=m(\gamma)$ for $\gamma\in\Gamma$, $\omega \in \Omega$. $F_m$ clearly satisfies $\| F_m \|_\infty \leq \| m \|_\infty$. Now
    \[
        \widehat m(g)=\frac1d\int_{\Omega} F_m(\omega g)\,d\omega
        =\frac1d\int_\mathrm{G} F_m(h)\1_{\Omega}(hg^{-1})\,dh.
    \]
    This expresses $\widehat{m}$ as a convolution of elements in $L_\infty(\mathrm{G})$ and $L_1(\mathrm{G})$ and thus it is bounded and continuous. 
            
    For the $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariance, we use that the geometric section above is the identity on the $\mathrm{K}$-part of the $\mathrm{ANK}$ decomposition. Thus, the fact that $\sigma(x k) = \sigma(x) k$ for every $k \in \mathrm{K}$ implies that
    \begin{align*}
        \beta(x,gk) =\beta(x,g) \quad \text{ and that } \quad
        \beta(x,kg) =\beta(xk,g).
    \end{align*}
    Hence, $\widehat m(gk)=\widehat m(g)$ follows immediately. For the right $\mathrm{K}$-action, we have 
    \[
        \widehat m(kg)
        =\int_{\Gamma \backslash \mathrm{G}} m(\beta(xk,g))\,d\mu(x)
        =\int_{\Gamma \backslash \mathrm{G}} m(\beta(x,g))\, d\mu(x)
        =\widehat m(g).
        \qedhere
    \]

body_md:
For \ref{itm:U-convergence1}, use spherical inversion 
    \[
\Theta^{-1}h(a_t) = \int_0^\infty h(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda(t) \, d\pi(\lambda)
    \]
    to get for  $\xi=R_j\lambda$ that
    \begin{align*}
        (U_jF)(s)
        &=\sqrt{e^{-R_js}\sinh(R_js)}
        \int_0^\infty F(\xi)w_j(\xi)
            \left(\frac{e^{R_js/2}}{R_j}
            \varphi_{\xi/R_j}(R_js)\right)\,d\xi.
    \end{align*}
    For fixed $s>0$ and according to Lemma~\ref{lem:spherical-limit}\ref{pslphase:eq:phi-bound}, we make take limits under the integral. The factor outside the integral tends to $1/\sqrt2$ while the weight $w_j(\xi)$ converges to $\pi\xi^2$. Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:spherical-limit}\ref{pslphase:eq:phi-limit} gives the limit of the factor in parenthesis. This justifies pointwise convergence. Moreover, weak $L_2$-convergence easily follows since $\{U_jF \colon j \ge 1\}$ is uniformly $L_2$-bounded, Now, the assertion follows by noticing that $\|U_jF\|_2 = \|F\|_{L_2(\mathbf{R}_+,d\pi_j)} \to \|F\|_{L_2(\mathbf{R}_+,d\pi_\infty)} = \|U_\infty F\|_2$ and $$\big\| U_\infty F - U_j F \big\|_{L_2(\mathbf{R}_+)}^2 = \big\| U_\infty F \big\|_{L_2(\mathbf{R}_+)}^2 + \big\| U_j F \big\|_{L_2(\mathbf{R}_+)}^2 - 2 \, \mathbf{Re} \, \big\langle U_\infty F ,U_j F \big\rangle \longrightarrow 0.$$ 

    For \ref{itm:U-convergence2}, conjugating $\mathcal{T}_{h_j}$ by the unitary $U_j$ gives the key identity

        \label{pslphase:eq:Aj-unitary}
        \Lambda_j=U_j^{-1}M_{h_j(a_{R_j\cdot})}U_j.

        =\int_0^\infty h_j(a_{R_js})(U_jF)(s)
                        \overline{(U_jG)(s)}\,ds.

    By \ref{itm:U-convergence1}, we obtain that $$\big\| U_\infty F\overline{U_\infty G} - U_jF\overline{U_jG} \big\|_{L_1(\mathbf{R}_+)} \to 0.$$ By the uniform boundedness of $|h_j|$, we can replace the product in the pairing by its limit.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m_z \colon \Gamma \to \mathbf{C}$ be the map $m_z(\gamma) = z^{d_T(o,\gamma \cdot o)}$. By Theorem \ref{Main Thm} we have that $M_z(x,y) = {z^{d_T(x,y)}}$ defines a family of uniformly completely bounded Schur multipliers on $S_p(T)$ for every $1 < p <\infty$. Denote by $\phi \colon \Gamma \to T$ the map $\gamma \mapsto \gamma \cdot o$ from $\Gamma$ into its Bass-Serre tree. Since $$m_z(\gamma^{-1} \eta) = z^{d_T(\eta \cdot o, \gamma \cdot o)} = M(\phi(\gamma), \phi(\eta))$$ and we know that the $S_p$-norm of the Schur multipliers with symbols $M$ and $M \circ (\phi \times \phi)$ is the same \cite[Section 1]{LaffSall2011}, we deduce that $\{m_z \colon |z|=1 \}$ defines a family of uniformly completely bounded Herz-Schur multipliers on $S_p(\Gamma)$. Its cocycle amplification $\widehat{m}_z$ is a continuous $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant function by Lemma \ref{lem:KbiinInduced} and, by \cite{LaffSall2011,WangXiaYao2025}, the uniform complete boundedness of $H_{\widehat{m}_z}$ on $S_p(\mathrm{G})$ is preserved.

    For the Fourier side, assume by contradiction that 
     \[
            \sup_{|z|=1} \big\| T_{\widehat{m}_z}\colon L_p(\mathcal{L} \mathrm{G}) \to L_p(\mathcal{L} \mathrm{G}) \big\| < \infty.
        \]
        Choose a sequence $R_j \to \infty$, phases $z_j = \exp(i \pi^2 / 12 R_j \log R_j)$ and fix $h_j(g) = \widehat{m}_{z_j}(g)$. According to Proposition~\ref{prp:cocycleWeakLaw}, we are in the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lem:U-convergence}. But the uniform boundedness of the multipliers $T_{\widehat{m}_z}$ on the Abelian corner $p_\mathrm{K} \, L_p(\mathcal{L} \mathrm{G}) \, p_\mathrm{K}$, together with \eqref{Eq-Spectral} and \eqref{Eq-Spectral2} plus Lemma \ref{lem:U-convergence}\ref{itm:U-convergence2} imply the boundedness of the operator $B_\Phi = U_\infty^{-1}M_{\Phi} U_\infty$ for $\Phi(s) = e^{is}$ on $L_p(d\pi_\infty)$. To obtain a contradiction, we will show that $B_\Phi$ is indeed unbounded. First, observe from \eqref{eq:Uinf} that $U_\infty = \mathcal{F}_{\sin} \circ \mathcal{V}$, where $\mathcal{V} \colon L_2(d \pi_\infty) \to L_2(d\xi)$ is the operator $(\mathcal{V} f)(\xi) \mapsto \sqrt{\pi} \xi f(\xi)$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\sin}$ is the odd part of the Fourier transform on $\mathbf{R}$
    \[
        (\mathcal{F}_{\sin} g)(s)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}
            \int_0^\infty g(\xi)\sin(\xi s)\,d\xi.
    \]
    Let $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbf{R}_+)$ be real-valued with support away from $0$ and set $F(x)=g(x)/x$. It holds that $x B_\Phi F(x)=\mathcal{F}_{\sin} \big( \Phi \mathcal{F}_{\sin} (g) \big)(x)$. Using Fourier inversion and taking real parts gives the following identity when $\Phi(s) = e^{is}$
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:translation-identity}
        \operatorname{\mathbf{Re}}\big(x B_\Phi F(x)\big)
        =\frac12\big[g_{\mathrm{odd}}(x+1)+g_{\mathrm{odd}}(x-1)\big] \quad \text{for} \quad x>0.
    \end{equation}
    Here $g_{\mathrm{odd}}$ is the odd extension of $g$. Now, fix a nonzero real-valued function
	\(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbf{R}_+)\) supported in $(1,2)$ and let \(0<\delta<1/4\).	
	Assume first that \(1\leq p<2\) and consider the functions 
	$
	g_\delta(x)=\psi(x/\delta)$ and $
	F_\delta(x)= g_\delta(x)/x$. Then we claim that  
    \[
        \frac{\|B_\Phi F_\delta\|_{L_p(d\pi_\infty)}}{\|F_\delta\|_{L_p(d\pi_\infty)}} \to \infty,
    \]
	which implies the assertion. To prove this claim note that
	\begin{equation*} 
		\|F_\delta\|_{L_p(d\pi_\infty)}^p
		=
		\pi \delta^{3-p}
		\int_1^2|\psi(u)|^p u^{2-p}\,du.
	\end{equation*}	When \(1+\delta<x<1+2\delta\), one has $
	g_\delta(x+1)=0$ and $
	g_\delta(x-1)
	=
	\psi\left(\frac{x-1}{\delta}\right)$. Thus \eqref{eq:translation-identity} gives
\begin{eqnarray*}		
\big\| B_\Phi F_\delta \big\|_{L_p(d\pi^2)}^p & \ge & \ \pi \int_{1+\delta}^{1+2\delta} \big| x B_\psi F_\delta(x) \big|^p \, x^{2-p} dx \\ 
		& \ge & \frac{\pi}{ 2^p}
		\int_{1+\delta}^{1+2\delta}
		\left|
		\psi\left(\frac{x-1}{\delta}\right)
		\right|^p
		x^{2-p}\,dx \ \ge \
		c_{p,\psi}\delta.
\end{eqnarray*}
	Thus
	\[
	\frac{\|B_\Phi F_\delta\|_{L_p(d\pi_\infty)}}
	{\|F_\delta\|_{L_p(d\pi_\infty)}}
	\geq
	c_{p,\psi}\delta^{(p-2)/p}
	\longrightarrow\infty,
	\]
	as claimed. The case \(p>2\) follows similarly for the same function $F_\delta(x) = g_\delta(x)/x$ but with the new choice \(g_\delta(x)=\psi((x-1)/\delta)\) and the interval \(\delta<x<2\delta\). In this case, we get the asymptotics reversed $\|F_\delta\|_p^p \approx \delta$ and $\|B_\Phi F_\delta\|_p^p \approx \delta^{3-p}$, which gives the right growth $\delta^{(2-p)/p}$ for $p>2$.

title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont
    As stated, Theorem \ref{CorSimple}\ref{itm:CorSimple2} just shows that there are  families of uniformly (completely) $S_p$-bounded Herz-Schur multipliers---with $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant symbols---that are non-uniformly bounded as Fourier multipliers over $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{R})$. However, given $p \in (1,\infty)\setminus \{2\}$, this easily implies that there are $\mathrm{K}$-biinvariant completely $S_p$-bounded Herz-Schur multipliers that are not bounded as Fourier multipliers on $L_p(\mathcal{L} \mathrm{PSL}_2 \mathbf{R})$. Indeed, for every $p \in [1,\infty]$ the Fourier multiplier norm bounds the Herz-Schur one---see the discussion around block B in the Introduction---and thus the identity map $m \mapsto m$ induces a contractive inclusion from Fourier multipliers into Herz-Schur ones. The graph of this contractive inclusion is closed and, by the closed graph theorem, the fact that we cannot bound the inverse map implies that the inclusion is not surjective.

title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont
    \label{rem:discrete-modular-phases}
    In fact, given $z\in \mathbf{T}$ and $p \in (1,\infty) \setminus \{2\}$ 
    \[
        \big\| T_{m_z}\colon L_p(\mathcal{L} \Gamma) \to L_p(\mathcal{L} \Gamma) \big\| \; < \; \infty
        \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad
        z^4 = 1.

This is not used in the proof of uniform unboundedness of $T_{\widehat{m}_z}$, nevertheless we include it for completeness. For the negative assertion, we restrict to the index-three subgroup $H= \ker q$, where $q:\Gamma = \mathrm{A} \ast \mathrm{B} \to \mathrm{B}$ sends $a$ to $e$ and fixes $\mathrm{B}$. Writing $c_j=b^jab^{-j}$ 
    \[
        H= \big\langle c_0,c_1,c_2\mid c_0^2=c_1^2=c_2^2=e \big\rangle \; \simeq \; \mathbf{Z}_2 \ast \mathbf{Z}_2 \ast \mathbf{Z}_2. 
    \]
    A reduced nonempty word is of the form $h=c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_n}$ with $i_j \neq i_{j+1}$ for $j \in \{1,2, \dots, n-1\}$ and thus corresponds to a word $b^{i_1} \, a \, b^{i_2-i_1} \, a \, \cdots \, b^{i_n-i_{n-1}} \, a \, b^{-i_n} \in \mathrm{A} \ast \mathrm{B}$. Counting the occurrences of $b^{\pm 1}$ gives
    \[
        \ell_T(h)=2\big[n-1+\1_{\{i_1\neq0\}}+\1_{\{i_n\neq0\}}\big].
    \]
    Thus, $m_z|_H$ is a radial phase with a correction depending on the first and last letters, rather than an exactly radial symbol in general.

    The Cayley graph of $H$ for these generators is the $3$-regular tree. Its radial algebra $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}$ is again generated by the sum of unit length elements $\chi_1$ and therefore Abelian. The spectral transform of $\chi_1/(2\sqrt2)$ identifies $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}$ with $L_\infty([-1,1],\nu_{2/3})$ and sends the normalized sphere sums $\chi_n/\|\chi_n\|_2$ to the orthonormal polynomials $Q_n$ considered in \eqref{eq:Qrecurrence} with parameter $\tau = \tfrac{2}{3}$, we refer to \cite{BoFen2006} for further details. Although $T_{m_z}$ need not preserve this algebra, its radial compression $\mathbf{E}_{\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}} T_{m_z}|_{\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}}$ is represented on radial polynomials, with $w=z^2$, by
    \[
        \mathbf{E}_{\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}} T_{m_z}|_{\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{rad}} \ \mapsto \  \mathscr{A}_z
        =\frac{(1+2w)^2}{9w}\mathcal J_w
        -\frac{4(w-1)^2}{9w}\mathcal J_{-\frac{w}{2}}
        +\frac{w^{-1}-1}{3}\Delta_0,
    \]
    where $\mathcal{J}_w Q_n=w^n Q_n$ and $\Delta_0 f= \nu_{2/3}(f) \, \1$. Since the conditional expectation is contractive, boundedness of $T_{m_z}$ would imply the boundedness of the compressed operator $\mathscr{A}_z$. 
    The last two terms are bounded on every $L_p(\nu_{2/3})$, whereas the coefficient of $\mathcal{J}_w$ is nonzero. Thus, the generating-function argument of Lemma~\ref{prop:generating} with $\tau=\tfrac{2}{3}$ makes the compression---as well as the multiplier $T_{m_z}$---unbounded whenever $z^4\neq1$ and $p\neq2$.

    For the converse $m_{\pm1}\equiv1$, while $m_{\pm i}$ is the product of the character $\chi(a)=-1$, $\chi(b)=1$ and a symbol determined by the first and last free factors in $\mathrm{A} \ast \mathrm{B}$. Thus, complete boundedness follows from \cite[Theorem~3.5]{MeiRicard2017FreeHilb}. At $p=1,\infty$, boundedness holds precisely when $z^2=1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We claim that 
\[
\varphi_n(x) := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \underbrace{\log \Big( \frac{1}{x_j^2} \Big)}_{\tau_j} \longrightarrow \frac{\pi^2}{6 \log 2} \quad \text{a.e. } x \in (0,1). 
\]
In fact, take $f(x,y, \varepsilon) = -2 \log(x)$. According to Lemma \ref{lem:arnoux-fd} \ref{lem:arnoux-fd3}, $\mathcal{R} \colon \Sigma \to \Sigma$ is measure preserving when $\Sigma$ is equipped with the probability measure $d\sigma(x,y,\varepsilon) = \tfrac{1}{2 \log 2} dx \, dy \, d \# (\varepsilon)$. Since $\mathcal{R} \colon \Sigma \to \Sigma$ is ergodic \cite[\S 5-6]{Arnoux1994}, Birkhoff's ergodic theorem applies to $f \circ \mathcal{R}^j$ and
\[
    \frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\tau_j
    \longrightarrow
    -2 \int_\Sigma \log x \, \frac{dx \, dy \, d \# (\varepsilon)}{2\log 2} =
    \frac{\pi^2}{6\log2},\quad  a.e.\  (x,y,\varepsilon) \in \Sigma.
\]
By the definition of \(n_t(z)\), we have \(n_t(z)\to\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\) and
	\[
	\frac{1}{n_t(z)}
	\sum_{j=0}^{n_t(z)-1}\tau_j
	<
	\frac{u+t}{n_t(z)}
	<
	\frac{1}{n_t(z)}
	\sum_{j=0}^{n_t(z)}\tau_j.
	\]
Taking the limit and combining it with Lemma
\ref{lem:khintchine} yields
\[
        \frac{n_t(z)}{t} \longrightarrow  		\frac{6\log2}{\pi^2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{1}{t\log t}
		\sum_{j=1}^{n_t(z)} d_j
		\longrightarrow
		\frac6{\pi^2}
\]
in measure. Lemma \ref{lem:return-cocycle} now yields the first assertion for the cocycle $\beta_0$. To pass from $\beta_0$ to a general $\beta$, let $\sigma \colon \Gamma \backslash \mathrm{G} \to \mathrm{G}$ be the section associated with $\beta$ by $\sigma(x)g=\beta(x,g)\sigma(xg)$. Write \(\sigma(z)=q(z)\sigma_0(z)\) for \(q(z)\in\Gamma\) so that $\beta(z,g)= q(z) \beta_0(z,g) q(zg)^{-1}$.
Hence
\[
	\big|
	\ell_T(\beta(z,a_t))
	-
	\ell_T(\beta_0(z,a_t))
	\big|
	\leq
	\ell_T(q(z))+\ell_T(q(za_t)).
\]
Since \(\mu\) is invariant under \(z\mapsto za_t\), we obtain 
	\[
	\mu\big\{
		z:
		\ell_T(q(za_t))>\eta t\log t
		\big\}
		=
		\mu\big\{
		z:
		\ell_T(q(z))>\eta t\log t
		\big\}
	\to 0,\quad \eta>0.
	\]
	Hence
	\[
	\frac{
		\ell_T(\beta(\cdot ,a_t))-\ell_T(\beta_0(\cdot,a_t))
	}{t\log t}
	\longrightarrow0
	\]
in probability. Together with the first assertion for $\beta_0$, this proves the desired convergence for the cocycle $\beta$. To conclude, let $R_j\to\infty$, $z_j = \exp ( i \pi^2/12R_j\log R_j)$ and fix \(s>0\). According to the first assertion and since $\log(R_js)/\log R_j \to 1$,
	we have
	\[
	m_{z_j}(\beta(\cdot,a_{R_js}))
	=
	\exp\left( 	i\frac{\pi^2\ell_T(\beta(\cdot,a_{R_js}))}
	{12R_j\log R_j}
	\right)
	\longrightarrow e^{i s}
	\]
	in \(\mu\)-probability.	
	Now, since
	\( m_{z_j}(\beta(\cdot,a_{R_js})) \) are uniformly bounded 
	\[
    \lim_{j \to \infty} \widehat m_{z_j}(a_{R_js})
		 = \lim_{j \to \infty}
			\int_{\mathrm{\Omega}}
			m_{z_j}(\beta(x,a_{R_js}))\,d\mu(x) =  e^{i s}. \qedhere
	\]
